17. Forward model summary

FY2026 GAAP operating income depends on an expected ~$10bn Q3 2026 accrual known only from press. The compute-sales line draws capacity from the same capex plan that supports the ad business, which management describes as short of compute, so that capacity is counted twice. And the base revenue path compounds at 14.7% a year for eight years, near the 80th-90th percentile of the reference class.

The model is an operating model from revenue to free cash flow. Year 0 is FY2025 and ties to the reported figures: FoA advertising $196,175M + FoA Other $2,584M + RL $2,207M = $200,966M; operating income $83,276M; capex including finance-lease principal $72,215M; free cash flow $43,585M. FY2026 is H1 reported plus an H2 projection.

17.1 What forces the construction

FoA advertising is built as prior-year revenue × (1 + DAP growth) × (1 + impressions-per-DAP growth) × (1 + price-per-ad growth). Other revenue, compute sales (GW sold × revenue per GW-year) and RL (glasses units × Meta revenue per unit + Quest units × $300 + store revenue) are separate lines. On the cost side, the two lines that the committed build sets in advance dominate:

  • Depreciation by capex vintage. Servers and network are 58% of capex (70% in service in the year, 5.5-year life), buildings 37% (placed over three years, 25-year life), other 5%; legacy assets run off from $21.6bn a year at Q4 2025. D&A rises from $29.9bn (FY2026E) to $71.2bn (FY2028E) and $143.2bn (FY2031E), 28.3% of revenue at its peak.
  • Infrastructure opex (third-party cloud, leases, power, AI tokens): $32.5bn in FY2026E [estimate: split of FoA "other costs"], +40% in 2027, +15% in 2028, fading to +5% by 2033, reflecting $81.65bn of commitments due in 2027 and $347bn of leases not yet commenced.

FY2026 bridge: H1 revenue $117,112M plus H2 $136,477M (ad growth +22.5%) gives $253,589M against consensus $254.1bn. Total costs of $177,082M are $167.1bn before the accrual, inside the $165-169bn guide. Operating income is $76,507M, $86.5bn before the accrual against consensus $86.7bn. Capex is $140.0bn and free cash flow −$4.9bn. On a GAAP basis the base does not meet management's "2026 operating income above 2025" statement, which was made before the settlement.

17.2 Assumptions and where each is contested

The revenue drivers each look defensible alone and are demanding together. In 2027 the base asks for DAP +2.5%, impressions per DAP +6.0% and price per ad +8.5% at once, about 17.9% ad growth, nine points above WPP's 2026 market forecast, and the 2033 terminal ad growth of about 8.2% keeps Meta gaining share for eight straight years. Meta's own record (revenue above year-end consensus in 12 of 13 years) is the counterweight, and the base is 1.7-1.9 points a year below consensus in 2027-2028. The cost side is more cautious than consensus (FY2029 operating margin 28.0% against 34-35%).

The evidence contradicts several assumptions:

  • Price per ad, 2027 (+8.5%) and 2028 (+7.0%). With 2024-2026 at 7% or more, the base makes 2024-2028 five straight years of 7%-plus price growth, against a longest positive run of three years (2016-2018). Price declined about 0.4% a year over 2018-2025 (Section 6.1) and declined in 4 of 10 years. Impressions per person rose while price declined in 2020, 2022 and 2023, and new low-priced surfaces coincided with price declines. 2027 laps the World Cup, the midterms and an H1 currency tailwind, and faces the teen non-personalised feed, EU less-personalised ads shown to virtually all EEA users, and the WhatsApp API interim measure. US & Canada price of +20% in Q2 2026 and 2024-25 prints of +10% and +9% keep 8.5% within reach. The evidence supports about 6-7% for 2027 (or 8.5% with impressions per DAP cut to about 4%) and about 5-6% for 2028.
  • DAP growth, 2027 (+2.5%). DAP went from 3.58bn (December 2025) to 3.60bn (June 2026), about +0.6% in the half (+1.1% annualised), against +3.9% in H1 2025 (3.35bn to 3.48bn). 2.5% needs net adds of about 90-100m a year against about 40m annualised now, with DAP at about 73% of internet users outside China and youth bans spreading. The evidence supports 1.5-2.0%, with the bear at 0-0.5%.
  • AI glasses units, 2027 (15m). The source the base cites contradicts it: IDC's path (13.6m in 2026 to 27.3m in 2030, about 19% a year) implies a 2027 category of about 16.2m; at a Meta share of 60-70%, falling as Android XR launches, that is 9.7-11.3m (11.6-13.4m on Omdia's higher base). The evidence supports about 12m; the revenue effect is about $0.4bn.
  • Meta revenue per glasses unit, 2033 ($160). IDC expects category ASP to decline about 39% to about $229 by 2030; Meta books about 25-50% of retail, which at $229 is about $57-115. The base raises Meta's take 28% while the retail price declines. The evidence supports about $90-125, with $160 plausible only if Meta books the Meta-branded line gross.
  • Glasses units, 2033 (35m). IDC's 19% category growth extended from 2030 gives about 46m in 2033; at 65% share that is about 30m. The evidence supports 25-30m.
  • Compute sold (0.5 GW from 2029) and its direct cost (40% of revenue). Management says Meta has "nowhere near enough compute" for its own uses and holds about $63bn of third-party cloud exposure, and no compute revenue, price or timeline is disclosed; the evidence supports 0 GW in the base with 0.5-2 GW as upside. The model carves the capacity out of the existing capex plan with no reduction in FoA drivers and no capacity charge. At about $43bn of capex per GW [estimate: $575bn of 2026-28 base capex over capacity rising from 7.5 GW to 21 GW per Wells Fargo], depreciation is about $5bn per GW-year, about 40% of $12bn of revenue, so an all-in cost of 75-85% of revenue is closer than 40%.
  • FoA Other revenue, 2033 (+15%, fading from +40%). The path compounds 2026's $4.26bn to about $23bn by 2033, about 5x, with no disclosed units; Morgan Stanley's subscription scenario (60m subscribers at $10 a month) is about $7bn, and the June 2026 EU interim measure targets WhatsApp business messaging. The evidence supports $12-18bn in 2033, with a bear terminal near 5%.
  • Infrastructure opex growth, 2027 (+40%, bear +45%) and 2028 (+15%). The 2026 base of $32.5bn is itself an estimate implying about 100% growth for that bucket; FoA non-D&A other costs rose 57% in H1 2026 before the legal charge; commitments due in 2027 are 53% above 2026's; and $347bn of unstarted leases imply $17-23bn a year of lease cost at full commencement against $2.8bn of operating lease cost in FY2025. The bear for 2027 should be about 55-60%, and 2028 about 20% (bear about 30%).
  • Compensation per FoA employee, 2027 (+12% in every scenario). Unrecognised RSU expense of $79.79bn recognised over about three years is about $26.6bn a year from existing grants, Q2 2026 stock compensation annualised to about $30.4bn, and the model's 2027 SBC of $30.9bn is below JPM's $33.0bn. The evidence supports +15-20%, with a range across scenarios.
  • RL program opex (−3% a year from 2027). RL costs rose every year 2019-2025, the 2022 promise to "pace" RL was met only at the consolidated level, VR savings were reinvested in wearables, and Q2 2026 costs were +3%. The evidence supports a flat base, with −3% as the bull.
  • Quest units (−10% a year) and Horizon store revenue (flat). VR shipments declined in 2022, 2023 and 2024, 14% in H1 2025 and 18% in Q2 2026, and Meta's headset share went from 72% to 54% after the April 2026 price rise; a −15% to −20% base and a declining store line fit better. Both are small in dollars.
  • Recurring legal charges ($3.0bn a year from 2027) and the settlement cash schedule ($1.0bn a year). 2026 legal charges total about $12.4bn; open matters include 200,000+ arbitration claimants, personal-injury and school-district bellwethers from October 2026 and February 2027, the New Mexico privacy case and EU DSA findings. The evidence supports $4-5bn a year with lumpy $10bn bear years, and settlement cash of about $1.3bn a year ($12.7bn fixed over ten years), with the $5.3bn contingent tranche as a bear item.
  • Capex change in 2029 (−8%). Meta's capex has declined y/y once in ten years (2023, after revenue declined); the base cuts 8% while revenue grows 15%, and Bloomberg has −3%. The evidence supports −3% to 0%; the base cut raises FY2029 free cash flow by about $10bn.
  • Server useful life (5.5 years; bear 5.0). Accelerator generations turn over every one to two years and the Q1 2026 10-Q added an impairment risk for excess infrastructure. The bear should be 4.0-4.5 years; at 4.5 years FY2029 operating income is $16.9bn lower.
  • Cost of new debt (5.8%). The base issues $86.0bn of notes in 2027 and $72.8bn in 2028, about 3x the largest prior issue, while the May 2026 20-40-year tranches priced at 6.20-6.45% and JV debt at 6.6-7.5%. The evidence supports 6.0-6.3%; the effect is about $0.3-0.6bn a year by 2029.
  • RSU withholding (65% of SBC in every scenario). The ratio was 50% (2023), 83% (2024), 90% (2025) and 64% (H1 2026) because it moves with the share price at vesting; one value ignores about ±$5-8bn a year of cash.
  • Dividend growth (+5% a year from 2027). The rate was held at $0.525 in 2026, and 2027-2028 are years of −$55bn and −$41bn of base free cash flow funded with new notes. The evidence supports 0% while free cash flow is negative.

The drivers that hold include H2 2026 ad growth (+22.5%; revenue has never come in below the guide's low end in 18 quarters). They also include impressions per DAP (+10.2% in 2026, +6.0% in 2027, +3.0% in 2033), 2026-2028 capex of $140bn, $210bn and $225bn (the post-print broker cluster is $214-243bn for 2027), the 2033 capex intensity of 30%, the 15% tax rate and net RSU issuance of 1.6% a year.

17.4 Reconciliation and consistency

The base margin declines from 41.4% to a trough of 27.1% in FY2031E because D&A rises from 9.3% to 28.3% of revenue and infrastructure opex from about 8% to 14-15%, while compensation and other opex fall as shares of revenue. Base operating income still grows every year from FY2027, which matches management's stated objective of operating-profit dollars. Base incremental operating margins are 20-33% in 2027-2031, against 42% for FoA in 2025 and 13% in H1 2026; no base or bull year exceeds the historical best (97% consolidated in 2023). Base D&A is close to consensus-implied D&A through FY2028 once Bloomberg's lease add-back is allowed for, and exceeds it from FY2029 ($96.2bn against $90.3bn). Base ARPP is within 1% of JPM's in each year to 2028; the base revenue gap to JPM in 2027 ($300.1bn against $305.3bn) comes from DAP.

Bloomberg capex and free cash flow exclude finance-lease principal, so like-for-like the base capex runs a few billion above and free cash flow a few billion below. Four differences explain the gap: - The Q3 accrual: the base books the ~$10bn Q3 accrual that most models, including JPM (10 September) and GS (13 September), exclude; before it, base FY2026 operating income ($86.5bn) matches consensus. - Other costs: consensus holds a 34-35% margin while its own implied D&A rises about 7 points of revenue by 2028, so it assumes other costs fall by about 7 points; the base holds infrastructure opex at 14-15% of revenue through 2029, a line no broker breaks out. - Revenue: base growth is 1.7-1.9 points a year below consensus in 2027-2028. - Debt: base cumulative FY2026-FY2028 free cash flow is −$100.8bn against −$36.3bn for consensus, so base net debt peaks at $204.8bn in FY2029 where GS models no new debt after 2026 and JPM $165.2bn of net debt by 2028.

1. AI infrastructure obligations. Meta has contracted capacity, leases and guarantees whose cash costs do not flex with ad demand. Commitments grew from $27.95bn (June 2025) to $349.31bn (June 2026), about 12x in twelve months, and $81.65bn falls due in 2027, about 70% of FY2025 operating cash flow. H2 2026 free cash flow is about −$34bn to −$4bn and FY2026 about −$20bn to +$10bn [estimate: H2 operating cash flow $60-75bn against remaining capex of $79-94bn]. Filing language changed in three successive quarters: - Q3 2025 10-Q: deleted "and thereafter for the foreseeable future" from the liquidity sentence and added "we may also seek to raise additional capital through debt, equity, or other financing arrangements". - Q1 2026 10-Q: added "any technical infrastructure in excess of our actual needs may lead to impairment of assets on our balance sheet". - Q2 2026 10-Q: added "We have incurred significant indebtedness and other contractual commitments, including lease obligations, to finance these investments and expect to continue to incur additional obligations."

Reported capex understates the build: after the Blue Owl venture closed, "the construction cost of the data center will not be recorded in CapEx" (Li, Q3 2025 call). Servers for 2028 are not yet ordered, which is the flexible part. Management's statements that capacity can be sold "at a significant premium" are claims and are not counted as mitigants.

2. Depreciation. The January 2025 life extension to 5.5 years cut FY2025 depreciation by $2.92bn. On $119.7bn of gross servers and network at June 2026, excluding $80.3bn of construction in progress, annual depreciation is about $21.8bn at 5.5 years, $29.9bn at 4 years and $39.9bn at 3 years [estimate: straight-line], and the base grows each quarter (Q2 2026 depreciation +40% y/y).

3. Youth safety. The 2026 events: - March: a $375m New Mexico jury penalty, and a first personal-injury bellwether award split 70/30 with YouTube. - Q2: $2.4bn of legal charges. - August: a $567m New Mexico abatement order with five years of court-supervised reforms (NMDOJ [web]), and the 26 August settlement with 52 attorneys general of "approximately $18 billion" over ten years, about $12.7bn fixed and $5.3bn released only if YouTube and TikTok adopt the same limits. The settlement imposes a combined 2-hour daily cap for under-18s, midnight-6am blocks, age assurance and a non-personalised feed option (Variety, NPR [web]).

Arbitration claimants rose from "over one hundred thousand" to "over two hundred thousand" in one quarter. Morgan Stanley estimates teens at about 1% of revenue with average teen time below the new cap (30 August 2026).

4. EU. The 10-K states less-personalised ads "are less relevant and effective than our premium ad offerings" and that further changes "could result in a materially worse user experience for European users and a significant impact to our European business and revenue". A January 2026 choice flow put that option in front of virtually all EEA users (ppc.land [web]). The June 2026 WhatsApp interim measure hits paid messaging, the main driver of Other revenue, and Meta AI's distribution on WhatsApp. Every 10% of European revenue is about $4.7bn [estimate]. The FTC's appeal is being briefed with 29 states supporting it (MediaPost, 2026-08-24 [web]).

5. Advertiser quality. The China and scam-ad exposures come from the same reseller-heavy cross-border e-commerce pool, so enforcement or trade action on either would hit impressions and price together. The FY2024 10-K first said stronger enforcement "will have an impact on our revenue in the future, which may be material", and the Q2 2026 10-Q rewrote the societal-harms paragraph to cover "deceptive activity or advertising, financial scams".

Risks that move together. A macro or tariff hit to e-commerce ads lowers operating cash flow while 2027 commitment payments and lease starts are fixed, at the moment credit markets would price Meta's risk higher. If Meta's models trail the frontier, external demand for its API and the option to resell compute shrink when capacity loosens, the same conditions that would surface depreciation-life questions. Youth caps, DSA findings on minors, EU less-personalised ads and any gatekeeper change all reduce targeting quality and price per ad through the same users. And settlement instalments (about $1.3bn a year), the New Mexico award, possible IRS payments and EU fines are cash calls in the heaviest capex years. In 2022 several of these risks arrived together: ATT, TikTok and the metaverse ramp, revenue −1%, operating margin 40% to 25%, and $4.61bn of restructuring charges including $1.34bn of data-centre assets.

Primary filings. Ten annual reports (FY2016-FY2025) and four earlier annual reports (FY2012-FY2015) pulled from EDGAR, the WhatsApp 8-K/A financial-statement exhibits (2014), quarterly reports for 2024-Q3, 2025-Q1 to Q3 and 2026-Q1 and Q2, nine DEF 14A proxy statements (2018-2026), the January 2026 8-K on the President's appointment, and four bond pricing term sheets (May 2023, August 2024, November 2025, May 2026). Peer and value-chain filings used directly: Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Apple, Snap, Pinterest, Reddit, The Trade Desk, AppLovin, NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Oracle, Garmin, Logitech, Sonos and GoPro, from their 10-Ks, latest 10-Qs and SEC XBRL company facts.

Transcripts and presentations. Thirty-eight earnings-call transcripts from Q1 2017 to Q2 2026 without a gap (Q2 2026 from S&P Capital IQ, the rest from BamSEC) and nineteen conference and special-event transcripts (Morgan Stanley TMT, Goldman Communacopia 2025, Connect 2025, annual meetings, the October 2022 special call). Seven decks: quarterly earnings presentations for Q3 2021, Q3 2023, Q3 2025, Q4 2025, Q1 2026 and Q2 2026, and Meta's 88-slide opening statement in FTC v. Meta (14 April 2025), which is litigation advocacy built from Meta data and Meta-retained experts.

Market and consensus data. Bloomberg terminal pulls dated 23 September 2026: daily price, high, low, total-return index, price-to-book and market capitalisation since the 2012 IPO; weekly one- and two-year-forward consensus EPS, sales and EBITDA; FY2012-FY2025 actuals and BEst consensus FY2025-FY2029 with dispersion; twelve quarters of actual against consensus with next-session reactions; monthly revision history; a 28-row comparable-company table; and a reference-class panel of 1,189 companies (S&P 500 members at seven dates since 1995 including delisted names, plus 25 non-US and internet names) with FY1990-FY2025 fundamentals. Sell-side: Morgan Stanley, J.P. Morgan, Goldman Sachs and TD Cowen reports dated 30 July to 13 September 2026, plus Deutsche Bank, Wells Fargo, Mizuho and Jefferies notes from June and July 2026; all are Buy or Overweight.

Other local sources. earnings-call guidance extractions (Q1 2018 to Q2 2026), a Daloopa workbook, 10-K risk-factor redlines FY2020-FY2025 and quarterly redlines, parsed proxy compensation data, Glassdoor snapshots (2020-2026) and Form 4 filings from 18 March to 3 June 2026.

Derived series. A ten-year annual history and a twelve-quarter series reconciled across XBRL, Daloopa and Bloomberg; monthly buyback purchases from 34 filings (2017-2025) priced against daily closes; a peer financial table from XBRL; a driver-based operating model with 52 drivers across three scenarios and a one-at-a-time sensitivity.

Gaps and failures. The settlement 8-K of August 2026 and other Q3 2026 filings are not in the archive, so the accrual and settlement terms come from press. The sell-side database server did not connect; the report digest was read directly and is dated 5 August 2026, with four later reports read from source files. Insider Form 4 data covers only March-June 2026. Proxy pay-versus-performance data for 2024-2026 were misparsed and the proxy text was used. Revenue by user geography is machine-readable only from Q4 2020, so annual user-geography series start in FY2021. Segment data starts in FY2019. Bloomberg's FY2016 GAAP consensus is thin. Earnings decks before Q3 2021 were available and not used. No filings exist for EssilorLuxottica, SK hynix, CoreWeave, Nebius, Blue Owl, ByteDance or OpenAI, so their figures are from press and company releases. The external datasets identified for this company were not collected (Appendix C).

Discrepancy log. - Capex: Bloomberg's FY2025 capex is $69,691M (purchases of property and equipment); Meta's figure including finance-lease principal is $72,215M. Bloomberg free cash flow ($46,109M) uses the narrower capex; Meta's is $43,585M. Forward consensus capex and free cash flow follow Bloomberg's definition. - Bloomberg EBITDA exceeds operating income plus D&A by the operating lease cost in each year from FY2019 ($2,798M in FY2025). - Bloomberg's net debt includes operating and finance leases ($3,489M net debt at FY2025) where the notes-only basis shows $22.6bn of net cash. - FY2016 capex is $4,491M in the annual history and $4,803M in the uses-of-cash table, which includes capital-lease principal; FY2016 free cash flow is $11,617M and $11,305M accordingly. - One-day declines are close-to-close price changes (−26.4% on 3 February 2022, −24.6% on 27 October 2022, −19.0% on 26 July 2018, −11.3% on 30 October 2025, −8.0% on 30 July 2026); market-capitalisation changes on the same days are larger because Bloomberg updates share counts on filing dates. - Quest 2025 units are estimated at 3.2-3.9m from one set of tracker inputs and 2.3-3.0m from another; the range used here is 2.3-3.9m. - Meta's glasses share is 85.2% (Omdia, FY2025, AI glasses), 82% (Counterpoint, H2 2025) and 69.2% (IDC, Q1 2026, smart glasses); the gap mixes a time change with category definitions. - The settlement is reported at $16.7bn (CNBC), about $17bn (NPR, Tennessee AG) and "approximately $18 billion" (Meta via Variety, $12.7bn fixed plus $5.3bn contingent). - Scale AI: $14.3bn reported for 49% against $13.79bn recorded in the Q3 2025 10-Q. - CoreWeave's Meta contract: $14.2bn (2025) and "up to $21bn" (September 2026 reports). - Consensus compute capacity at year-end 2025: about 3GW owned (MS, TD Cowen) against 7.5GW (Wells Fargo), a definitional difference between owned and total. - Q2 2026 EPS consensus: $7.15 (BEst GAAP) against $7.10 in dated press.

Internal discrepancies. Five quantities appear on two bases here. - ROIC: Section 3 uses operating income at a uniform 21% tax rate over invested capital (35.2% for FY2025, 28.6% trailing to June 2026); Section 13 uses an adjusted tax rate that excludes the discrete charges (39.4% for FY2025; about 31% trailing). The Section 3 series is used for the peer comparison. - Net debt: notes-only net cash of $6.3bn (Sections 10 and 12), net debt including operating leases of $22.1bn (front matter), and debt plus finance leases less cash of −$21.7bn at FY2025 (Section 13). The front matter's net cash without leases ($6,596M) nets the notes at their $83,664M carrying value; Sections 10 and 12 use the $84,000M face value. - Meta's revenue per glasses unit: $95-170 on the residual method alone, $150-200 on a separate incremental method, and $95-200 as the combined range used here. - FoA gross margin of 83.0-83.5% recomputes to 83.1-83.6% on the same inputs. - The 2026 price per ad is +10.9% in every scenario in the model's stated assumptions and +8.72% in its bear projection.

Unresolved internal conflicts. These pairs of figures cannot be settled from the document itself. - Capex and free cash flow, FY2016 and FY2020-FY2022: the uses-of-cash table (Section 10.4) shows capex of $4,803M, $15,767M, $19,367M and $32,281M and free cash flow of $11,305M, $22,980M, $38,316M and $18,194M; the annual history (Section 13.1) and the Section 3 ROIC table show $4,491M, $15,719M, $19,244M and $32,036M and $11,617M, $23,028M, $38,439M and $18,439M. Sections 3, 13.1 and 13.3 use the annual-history basis, the Section 10.4 per-share arithmetic (capex 17.4% of 2016 revenue, FCF per share +17.8% a year) uses the uses-of-cash basis, and the Section 12.3 leverage table mixes them (FY2021 FCF $38.3bn, FY2022 $18.4bn). - Q2 2026 stock compensation is $7,658M (+58%) in Section 13.3 and $7.60bn (+57%) in Section 12.4; Section 17.2 annualises the $7.60bn figure. - FY2016 RSU withholding-tax cash is $6M in Section 12.4 and $0 in Section 10.4. - After the Q3 2025 print the FY2027 free-cash-flow consensus declined from $41.7bn to $28.2bn "in a month" (Section 15.3) and to $27.1bn by 20 November 2025 (Section 15.4); the reading dates are not given precisely enough to reconcile them. - Reality Labs 2026 costs are $21.5-22.5bn in the Section 1.1 FoA-cost arithmetic and a $21-22bn base in the Section 1.2 wearables and VR split. - RL revenue-mix estimates differ by section. Section 1.2 puts FY2025 Meta-booked glasses revenue at $0.66-1.18bn and Quest hardware at $0.83-1.25bn, while its residual bullet uses Quest inputs of 2.3-3.9m units at $250-330 (about $0.58-1.29bn); Section 4.2 shows RL-booked glasses revenue of ~$0.7-1.3bn and Quest hardware of ~$0.6-1.25bn. Meta glasses consumer spend is ~$2.4-2.8bn in the Section 4.2 table and $2.1-2.7bn in Section 5. The Section 1.2 mix table, which sums to $2,207M, is the basis used elsewhere. - Section 11 says regulators intervened in three of "the seven acquisitions since 2019 with a reported price"; the Section 11 deal table lists five acquisition rows since 2019 (CTRL-labs, Giphy, Kustomer, Within, and Manus with others) plus three minority stakes. - The estimates paragraph below counts about seventy estimates; the text carries about ninety-four [estimate tags, some repeated for one figure across table cells. - Section 18 gives Q2 2026 depreciation growth of +40% y/y and Section 13.3 D&A growth of +46%; the depreciation-only figures are not shown.

Corrections. Giphy was acquired for $315M, so the $53M sale recovered about 17% of cost. The El Paso SPV notes priced at 7.534%, about 95bp over Hyperion's 6.581%. Q1 2026 revenue growth of 33% was the fastest since Q3 2021 (35%). Q2 2026 price-per-ad growth of 12% was below Q4 2024's 14%. Cumulative RL losses through June 2026 are $96,725M, including Q1 2026's $4,028M.

Estimates by method. About seventy figures are tagged [estimate: …], each with its bounds. By method: - Residual or triangulation (about twenty): undisclosed units and splits, including impression levels and CPMs, FoA gross margin, Meta's revenue per glasses unit, Quest units, the RL revenue mix and gross margin, the China-advertiser range and infrastructure opex in FY2025-26. - Guide or consensus arithmetic (about fifteen): 2026 FoA costs and incremental margin, FY2026 operating income with the accrual, H2 and FY2026 free cash flow, and headcount after the Q3 exits. - Market sizing and concentration (about twelve): glasses and VR consumer spend, HHIs, the social-ad pool, cost-to-market multiples and consensus-implied global share. - Balance sheet (about eight): lease present value, lease-adjusted leverage, lease cost at commencement, depreciation at shorter lives and capitalised interest. - Value chain (about eight): splits of the capex dollar and supplier gross profit. - Returns and per-share arithmetic (the rest): return on the 2023-25 build, FoA ROIC, WhatsApp's deal multiple and share value, buybacks needed to hold the count, net issuance and the AMD warrant sensitivity.

Web sources. About fifty distinct domains are cited, in five groups: industry trackers and agencies (IDC, Omdia, Counterpoint, WPP Media, eMarketer, IAB/PwC, WARC, ITU); business and technology press (CNBC, Bloomberg, Reuters via secondary outlets, Fortune, TechCrunch, The Register, Axios, Yahoo Finance, Motley Fool, 9to5Mac, 9to5Google, UploadVR, mixed-news); company and investor-relations pages (EssilorLuxottica, AMD, SK hynix, TSMC, Meta newsroom, Google blog, OpenRouter, Artificial Analysis); legal and regulatory sources (NMDOJ, FTC, Variety and NPR on the settlement, MediaPost, ppc.land); and bond-market coverage (IFR, cbonds, El Paso Matters). Every web-sourced claim is listed in Appendix B with its link and access date. Two claims are marked [web, unverified] because the source could not be re-fetched: China-based advertisers at about 10-11% of 2024 revenue, and the internal projection that 10.1% of 2024 revenue came from scam and banned-goods ads.

External datasets. None were collected. Appendix C lists the two identified for this company.

20. What we still don't know, and the metrics that would resolve it

The first two gaps change the conclusions of Sections 1, 3 and 17.

  1. What share of impression growth is ad load, and which apps account for it. Impressions per person rose about 12-13% in H1 2026, more than double the 2025 rate of about 5%, and the 10-Q names "the frequency of ads shown"; the split between time spent and ads per minute, and between Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads, is undisclosed. Instagram is about 40% of ad revenue on eMarketer's estimate. Impressions per DAP is the model's largest sensitivity (about ±$31bn of FY2033E operating income per point a year). Resolves with: per-app revenue or ad-load disclosure; third-party time-spent panels by app (Appendix C).
  2. How much of the 2026 build serves ads ranking and how much frontier-model training. Meta Superintelligence Labs, its talent packages, the March 2026 option grant and third-party AI token costs are all inside FoA; Li said "a substantial amount of the compute goes towards training models" (Q2 2026 call). Whether the FoA incremental margin decline (83% in 2024 to 13% in H1 2026) is a lower return in the ad system or spending on a separate program depends on the split. Resolves with: a cost or capacity split between ads and MSL, cluster designations (Prometheus, Hyperion) or MSL headcount and compensation.
  3. The settlement accrual and whether "2026 operating income above 2025" survives. The ~$10bn Q3 accrual and settlement terms come from press. Resolves with: the August 2026 8-K and the Q3 2026 10-Q.
  4. Advertiser mix by size, vertical and origin. US & Canada, where price per ad rose 20%, supplied 49% of Q2 2026 ad revenue growth, and the base-rate downside for price is 2022's −16%. Which cohorts (SMB, large brand, app-install, retail, China-based cross-border sellers) pay the higher prices sets how cyclical the gain is. The billing-versus-user gap ($14.6bn in FY2025) exists as a series from FY2021 and would show whether the cross-border cohort is shrinking. Resolves with: vertical or advertiser-size disclosure; the billing-versus-user series through the May 2025 de minimis change.
  5. Where ad load stands against its ceiling. Meta has disclosed no ads-per-session measure, and the base fades impressions per person from 10.2% (2026) to 6% (2027). Resolves with: third-party ad-load measurement or a management statement of headroom.
  6. The under-18 share of DAP, time spent and revenue. The settlement's 2-hour cap, the New Mexico reforms and under-16 bans act through this base; Morgan Stanley estimates teens at about 1% of revenue. Resolves with: a disclosure, or Teen Accounts counts against census age structure.
  7. Whether Advantage+ revenue is incremental. The >$75bn run rate is about 32% of ad revenue and is management's main evidence that AI is paying off; the share migrated from manual campaigns is undisclosed. Resolves with: an incremental-spend or advertiser-cohort disclosure.
  8. Emerging-market monetisation. Nearly all DAP growth now comes from markets such as India, Indonesia, Brazil and Nigeria, at about a twelfth of US & Canada ARPU at the last disclosure (Q4 2023). Whether WhatsApp-led monetisation narrows the gap sets the 2-point mix drag on worldwide price. Resolves with: regional DAP or ARPU, discontinued in 2024.
  9. How price per ad behaves in a demand-led ad recession. The downside base rates are 2020 (−10%) and 2022 (−16%, ATT plus macro); a recession without a signal shock against $81.65bn of fixed 2027 commitments has no reference in Meta's own history. Resolves with: the 2001 and 2008-09 ad-market record (Google, IAB) as an external reference.
  10. Meta's economics on EssilorLuxottica-sold glasses. Whether Meta sells a module, takes a revenue share or books the Meta-branded line gross decides whether glasses volume can close any of the RL loss. Resolves with: disclosure by either company; RL revenue by product line.
  11. The commencement schedule and lease/finance split of $347bn of unstarted leases, and the counterparty split of $349bn of commitments. These set the path of infrastructure opex and depreciation. Resolves with: the lease and commitments notes in the FY2026 10-K.
  12. The economic life of AI servers against the 5.5-year book life. Resolves with: any change-in-estimate note, impairment of excess capacity, or peer life changes.
  13. Who succeeds Zuckerberg, and what external check exists on capital allocation. He holds 60.8% of the vote and decides a $130-145bn capex program in which he bears 13.5% of the economics; the board cannot replace him. Resolves with: a succession disclosure; dual-class and say-on-pay vote results by class.
  14. TikTok's US trajectory under the USDS joint venture. TikTok is the largest share threat, and only WARC's $14.5bn 2026 US forecast exists. Resolves with: third-party ad-revenue estimates and advertiser surveys after January 2026.
  15. Insider trading before 2026 and the bearish sell-side case. Insider transactions are known only for March-June 2026, and the brokers cited all rate Meta Buy or Overweight. Resolves with: multi-year Form 4 history through the 2022 drawdown; a Neutral- or Sell-rated driver model.

Monitoring metrics, in the order they would turn. US & Canada price per ad (+20% in Q2 2026), the most direct measure of ranking gains with no currency effect. Worldwide impressions growth against DAP growth plus about 5 points (+14% against +3%). FoA Other revenue (+73%), the test of non-ad revenue. The Q3 2026 revenue print against the $61-64bn guide, where a result at or below the low end would mean 2026 share gains were partly cyclical. Europe ad growth against the total (+24% against +27.5%), where a gap above 10 points would show less-personalised ads constraining revenue. The quarterly commitments and unstarted-lease lines, restricted cash and new-issue spreads on Meta notes. The 2027 capex guide in late January 2027. FoA segment margin, and the RL loss against "similar to 2025". Family DAP for two consecutive q/q declines not explained by country shutdowns. Any disclosed compute, API or business-agent revenue.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Meta has held no investor day, and its quarterly decks are chart versions of the 10-Q tables with one addition: ad impression and price-per-ad growth by user geography as numbers. The FTC trial deck is the richest source, containing Meta's internal engagement data; every slide in it is advocacy prepared for litigation from Meta data and Meta-retained experts.

What the decks add

  • Friend content is a small share of time. Friends' posts were 22% of Facebook time and 11% of Instagram time in 2023, and 17% and 7% in 2025, so recommended and followed content is more than 80% of time on both apps [deck: FTC v. Meta opening statement 2025-04-14, slides 20-21] (§1, §3, §4).
  • Video took over Facebook. Video rose from about 11% of US Facebook time (January 2015) to about 53% (January 2025) [deck: FTC v. Meta 2025-04-14, slide 38] (§2).
  • Instagram as a messaging app. Adam Mosseri in deposition: "I think [Instagram]'s more of a messaging app than a broadcast-sharing app at this point" [deck: FTC v. Meta 2025-04-14, slide 46]. Private sharing moved into messages, which show no feed ads, and business messaging is how Meta monetises it (§1).
  • Per-app US users. US monthly users grew from 159m to 236m on Facebook and from 3.9m to 217m on Instagram between 2012 and 2022, and Instagram had "230M+" US users in 2025 [deck: FTC v. Meta 2025-04-14, slides 11 and 80] (§1).
  • Time share depends on the market drawn. About 85% in the FTC's market, below 60% with TikTok, about 30% with YouTube, below 30% with both and below 20% with iMessage and other apps [deck: FTC v. Meta 2025-04-14, slides 67-72] (§4).
  • Natural experiments point to YouTube and TikTok. During the January 2025 TikTok shutdown usage rose 20% on Facebook, 17% on Instagram and 14% on YouTube; during the October 2021 Meta outage it rose 11% on TikTok and 8% on YouTube; with Instagram blocked in a 2023 field study, YouTube gained 19% and Facebook 13%. Snap gained 0.5-4% in every test [deck: FTC v. Meta 2025-04-14, slides 28-32] (§4).
  • R&D intensity. Meta's R&D was about $38bn in 2023, up from under $1bn in 2011, and about 29% of revenue in 2022-2023 against about 13-15% at Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft [deck: FTC v. Meta 2025-04-14, slides 13-14; values read off the chart] (§3).
  • Consumer surplus. Carlton estimated $38.5-110bn a year from Instagram and WhatsApp combined [deck: FTC v. Meta 2025-04-14, slide 86], a measure of how far user value exceeds the zero price (§18).
  • Regional price and volume. US & Canada price per ad +20% on impressions +9% in Q2 2026; Asia-Pacific impressions +16-24% for five quarters at price −2% to +5% [deck: Meta Earnings Presentation Q2 2026 2026-07-29, slides 12-13] (§1).
  • Mix lowers the worldwide price. A revenue-weighted average of regional price growth was about 14% in Q2 2026 and 8% in Q4 2025 against 12% and 6% reported, about 2 points of dilution from Asia-Pacific impression mix [estimate] (§1).
  • Impression growth decelerated in every region in Q2 2026, from 19% to 14% worldwide and from 23% to 17% in Asia-Pacific, while price growth held at 12% (§1, §13).

Appendix C — External data sources

Two external datasets fit a business of this shape. Neither was collected, and both would test quantities Meta does not disclose.

Google Trends — relative search interest. Not pulled. What it is: a weekly index of search volume for brand and product terms, by country. What it measures: consumer intent toward Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp, Threads, Meta AI and Muse, and toward TikTok, YouTube, ChatGPT and competing glasses brands, independent of company reporting. How it would inform this analysis: it would give a cheap independent series on whether consumer interest in Meta's apps is holding against TikTok and AI assistants (§4.1, §6.3), and whether Muse's September 2026 App Store ranking reflects sustained interest (§2). For Reality Labs, search interest in Ray-Ban Meta against Android XR and Chinese brands after the fall 2026 launches would be the earliest indicator of glasses share (§4.2). Search interest measures intent, not usage or revenue.

App and web engagement panels — downloads, daily and monthly users, time spent, sessions. Not pulled; partial mosaic, not comprehensive. What it is: third-party measurement of app installs, active users and time spent from device panels and app-store data (Sensor Tower, data.ai, Comscore, Similarweb), available here only as scattered cited data points. What it measures: engagement by app, country and cohort. How it would inform this analysis: the largest unknown in §1 is how much of the acceleration in impressions per person in H1 2026 (about +12-13%) came from more time spent and how much from more ads per minute, and per-app time spent is an independent check on management's "Instagram time spent up double digits" claim (§1, §3.1). Time share against TikTok, YouTube and ChatGPT by app would test the substitution evidence in §4.1 outside Meta's trial exhibits, and a panel of under-18 usage would help size the effect of the settlement's 2-hour cap (§18, §20).
